title: The first words after
hookLine: he returns and says there is no Hindu and no Muslim, and the town asks what he means
last: THREE DAYS IN THE RIVER — SOME COME BACK CHANGED.

cards: The whole town has mourned him. They dragged the river. His sister wept.
Then, on the third morning, he walks back into Sultanpur, alive, soaking wet, with a look on his face nobody can read. People crowd around. Where were you?
What happened? Are you all right? The stories say he didn't answer.
For a while he said nothing at all. He gave away what he owned and sat in silence. When he finally spoke, it wasn't an explanation.

teach.h: THERE IS NO HINDU, THERE IS NO MUSLIM.
teach.b: Here's the sentence, as tradition remembers it: there is no Hindu, there is no Muslim.

teach.h: A TOWN WHERE LABELS WERE EVERYTHING.
teach.b: You met it on day six, as that day's line; this is where it comes from.
Sultanpur had a Muslim governor, Hindu merchants and Muslim officials, temples and mosques, each community with its own rules about food, prayer and who you could marry.
Who you were showed in your food, your prayers, your clothes. And the storekeeper back from the dead says: neither. What did he mean?
The sources give no footnote, so Sikhs and scholars hear it in several ways.

teach.h: NO LABELS, A CHALLENGE, A NEW PATH.
teach.b: Some hear: before God, there are no labels. Beneath the Hindu and the Muslim are just people, all made by the one, Ik Onkar.
Others hear a challenge: nobody around him was truly living up to what their faith asked, and he was calling both back to the heart of their own paths.
And some hear the first sign of a new path, one defined by neither community. The readings don't cancel each other out; they can be held together.
What the sentence clearly isn't is contempt.

Nanak spent the rest of his life sitting with Hindus and Muslims, praying, singing, eating, arguing gently, and his companion on the road, Mardana, was a Muslim. Of course the town asked what he meant.
And the town's religious judge, the qazi, decided to find out for himself.

how: Sikhs remember Guru Nanak's words after the river as the start of his mission, and often quote them as a teaching that all people are one before God.

stay silent, then say: there is no Hindu, there is no Muslim.
go straight back to work at the storehouse.
games.why: the stories say he was silent, gave away what he owned, and then spoke one sentence that set the town talking.

practice: Bring to mind one real person you usually see through a label: liberal, conservative, rich, poor, old, young, religious, not.
Set the label down and look underneath, at someone who gets tired, who loves someone, who is afraid of something. Stay with that person, without the label, for a few slow breaths.
